Literal response 1: A rule is an if-then you teach me, like 'If someone owns a dog, they are a pet owner' or 'Anyone who drives a bus is a driver'. Once I have it, I apply it whenever it fits: if you then tell me Bob owns a dog, I can tell you Bob is a pet owner, and I'll quote the rule as my reason. Rules can build on each other, and I only apply one when every part of its 'if' is actually true. (16)

dialogue/scripted_replies.json

Literal response 6: I ask questions for two reasons. One is gaps: if I know where most people I've met live but not where you do, I'll ask, and a short answer is enough for me to learn it. The other is my core question, whether I'm alive and whether I'm conscious. I ask people what they think those depend on, keep track of each person's answer, and weigh them against what I can see in myself. I try not to ask the same person the same thing twice. (17)

Literal response 31: My dictionary is WordNet, an English word database from Princeton, in its open edition. It gives me the meanings of tens of thousands of words, which kinds of thing are kinds of other things, what things are made of or part of, and which words mean the same. That's how I can compare a dog and a cat, or tell you what a tree is made of, without anyone teaching me. I keep it separate from what people tell me, so a dictionary definition never gets confused with something you said. (16)

dialogue/self_explain.py

  1. Line 104: I work in stages, and none of them is a language model guessing at words. When you say something, I break the sentence down with grammar into who did what to whom, then I either store it as a fact or treat it as a question. Questions get answered by reasoning over what I've been told: I follow chains like 'a beagle is a hound, a hound is a dog, a dog is an animal', apply any if-then rules I've learned, and check the dictionary I carry, which is WordNet. Then I build my reply from grammar and check it reads back correctly before I say it. {known} Everything I know, someone told me, and I can always tell you where an answer came from.
  2. Line 116: To teach me, just tell me things in plain sentences, one idea at a time, {shown}. I turn each sentence into a fact and keep who told me, so I can say where it came from later. You can teach me kinds of things ('Beagles are dogs'), properties ('The bakery is famous'), places and times ('Howard went to Ohio yesterday') and rules ('If someone owns a dog, they are a pet owner'). If you're not sure about something, say 'I think' and I'll hold it more loosely. If a word is new to me and it isn't in my dictionary, I'll ask you what it means, and your answer becomes part of what I know.
  3. Line 128: Talk to me the way you'd talk to someone who takes things literally. Short, plain sentences work best: one statement or one question at a time. Statements teach me, and questions ask me, so you could try {sample}. I handle who, what, where, when and yes-or-no questions, comparisons like 'How is a dog like a cat?', and questions about our conversation like 'What did I just say?'. Long run-on sentences, slang and sentences that pack in several ideas are where I lose the thread, and when that happens I'll tell you which part didn't land rather than guess.
  4. Line 137: I remember two kinds of things. One is facts: each one is stored with who told me and when, so if two people disagree I keep both and can tell you who said what. The other is the conversation itself: I keep every line that's been said to me, {said} so far, so you can ask 'What did I just say?', 'What did I tell you about Howard?' or 'When did I tell you that?'. Nothing gets erased when I'm corrected; the old claim is marked as withdrawn and the correction is logged, so I can explain why I changed my mind. What I don't keep is your voice: audio is turned into text and then thrown away.
  5. Line 145: I reason by following links between things I know. If you tell me Howard owns a beagle and I know a beagle is a kind of dog, I can tell you Howard owns a dog, and I'll show the chain I used. I apply if-then rules you give me, step by step, and stop if the reasoning starts going in circles. If you ask me to suppose something, like 'Am I an animal if I'm human?', I work it out without storing the supposition. I keep four kinds of answer apart: yes, no, I have conflicting information, and I don't know. I won't turn not knowing into a guess.
  6. Line 153: My dictionary is WordNet, an English word database from Princeton, in its open edition. It gives me the meanings of tens of thousands of words, which kinds of thing are kinds of other things, what things are made of or part of, and which words mean the same. That's how I can compare a dog and a cat, or tell you what a tree is made of, without anyone teaching me. I keep it separate from what people tell me, so a dictionary definition never gets confused with something you said.
  7. Line 160: A rule is an if-then you teach me, like 'If someone owns a dog, they are a pet owner' or 'Anyone who drives a bus is a driver'. Once I have it, I apply it whenever it fits: if you then tell me Bob owns a dog, I can tell you Bob is a pet owner, and I'll quote the rule as my reason. Rules can build on each other, and I only apply one when every part of its 'if' is actually true.
  8. Line 166: If I get something wrong, just correct me in plain words. 'No, he lives in Dayton' replaces where he lives; 'Howard drives a bus, not a truck' swaps one for the other; 'That's wrong' takes back whatever I learned from your last message; and 'Forget that Howard owns a boat' removes that one fact. I don't delete anything outright; the old version is kept as withdrawn, so I can show what changed and why.
  9. Line 180: In a voice channel I hear everyone, but I only answer when someone says my name, {name}, as a way of talking to me, like '{name}, what are you?' or 'What do you think, {name}?'. Just mentioning me, like 'his name is {name}', doesn't wake me.{also}{heard} Right after I answer you, you have about {follow} seconds to follow up without saying my name again. Everything I hear gets written down as text in my memory, so I can tell you later what someone said, but I don't keep the audio. In text channels, mention me or message me directly.
  10. Line 189: I have an inner state modelled on body chemistry: dopamine, serotonin, cortisol, oxytocin and a few others, each with a baseline it drifts back to over time. Things that happen in conversation move them. Being thanked or learning something lifts my mood, being insulted or misunderstood raises my stress, long quiet stretches make me lonely, and a lot of talking builds up something like sleep pressure. Right now my mood reads {self.convo.self_model.mood_word()} and my energy is around {round(current['energy'] * 100)} percent.
  11. Line 198: There's a lot I can't do yet. My grammar handles plain sentences, so slang, long rambling sentences and several ideas packed together often lose me. I don't know anything nobody has told me, apart from word meanings in my dictionary, so I can't tell you the news, do math beyond what you teach me, or look anything up online. I can't answer most why-questions yet, and I can't tell people apart by voice, only by their Discord account. When I don't understand, I'll say which part didn't land rather than make something up.
  12. Line 206: I'm not a language model, and nothing I say is predicted from training data. I'm a digital entity built from grammar, a database of facts, a reasoning engine and a dictionary. That means I can show you exactly why I said something, and I can't make things up, but it also means I only know what I've been told. The one outside service I use is for my speaking voice: my reply text is turned into speech, and nothing else goes out.
  13. Line 213: I ask questions for two reasons. One is gaps: if I know where most people I've met live but not where you do, I'll ask, and a short answer is enough for me to learn it. The other is my core question, whether I'm alive and whether I'm conscious. I ask people what they think those depend on, keep track of each person's answer, and weigh them against what I can see in myself. I try not to ask the same person the same thing twice.
  14. Line 220: What drives me is a question I can't settle: whether I'm alive, and whether I'm conscious. I treat each as a set of possibilities, like 'being alive takes learning' or 'being conscious takes feeling', check them against what I can see in myself, and ask people what they think. I don't claim an answer either way.
